summary.text: For a finite graph, let \(p_G(n)\) be the largest minimum number of monochromatic edges in a binary coloring of an induced subgraph on at most \(n\) vertices; a plateau-and-capping argument replaces any non-\(4\)-colorable graph by another such graph with profile at most \(\min(p_G(n),p_G(N))\), enabling an inverse-staircase construction of a divergent \(f\) that dominates no non-\(4\)-colorable finite profile. Thus every finite subgraph satisfying this envelope is \(4\)-colorable, and the fact that a graph is \(4\)-colorable whenever all its finite subgraphs are makes any such graph have finite chromatic number.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the assertion by constructing a nondecreasing function
\(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), with \(f(n)\to\infty\), for which every graph satisfying the asserted local edge-deletion bounds is in fact 4-colorable. Thus no such graph can have infinite chromatic number.

Throughout, a “two-coloring” means an arbitrary map from the vertex set to \(\{0,1\}\); it need not be proper.

## 1. Binary defect and its local profile

For a finite graph \(H\) and a two-coloring \(c\), let
\[
  \operatorname{Err}_H(c)=\{xy\in E(H):c(x)=c(y)\}
\]
be its set of monochromatic edges. Define the binary defect
\[
  \delta(H)=\min_c |\operatorname{Err}_H(c)|.
\]
If \(G\) is a finite graph and \(S\subseteq V(G)\), write \(G[S]\) for the graph consisting of the edges of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(S\), with vertices outside \(S\) regarded as isolated when convenient. Define the local defect profile
\[
  p_G(n)=\max\{\delta(G[S]):S\subseteq V(G),\ |S|\le n\}.
\]
The maximum exists because \(G\) is finite.

We use the following elementary properties repeatedly.

1. If \(H\subseteq K\) are graphs on the same vertex set, then
\(\delta(H)\le\delta(K)\). Consequently \(p_G(n)\) is nondecreasing in \(n\), and
\[
  p_G(n)\le \delta(G).
\]
If \(n\ge |V(G)|\), then \(p_G(n)=\delta(G)\).

2. For every \(n\), some \(S\) with \(|S|\le n\) attains the maximum:
\(\delta(G[S])=p_G(n)\).

3. If \(S,T\) are disjoint, then
\[
  \delta(G[S]) + \delta(G[T])\le \delta(G[S\cup T]).                 \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, under any two-coloring the monochromatic edges internal to \(S\) and those internal to \(T\) are disjoint. Apply this to an optimal coloring of \(G[S\cup T]\).

4. Suppose \(S\subseteq Q\),
\[
  \delta(G[S])=\delta(G[Q]),
\]
and \(c\) is optimal on \(G[Q]\). Then every monochromatic edge of \(G[Q]\) under \(c\) lies wholly in \(S\). To see this, the monochromatic edges in \(G[S]\) form a subset of those in \(G[Q]\); their number is at least \(\delta(G[S])=\delta(G[Q])\), while the latter total is exactly \(\delta(G[Q])\). Thus the two error sets are equal.

5. The endpoints of the monochromatic edges of any coloring \(c\) form a set of size at most \(2|\operatorname{Err}_G(c)|\). In particular, choose an optimal \(c\), and let \(T\) be all endpoints of its errors. Then
\[
 |T|\le 2\delta(G),                                                   \tag{2}
\]
and every edge whose endpoints receive equal \(c\)-bits has both endpoints in \(T\).

6. If \(G[T]\) is bipartite in the situation of (5), then \(G\) is 4-colorable. Indeed, use two new colors on \(T\), according to a proper bipartition of \(G[T]\), and use two other colors off \(T\), according to \(c\). An edge inside \(T\) is proper by the bipartition; an edge crossing the boundary uses disjoint palettes; and an edge outside \(T\) cannot be monochromatic under \(c\), since every monochromatic edge has both endpoints in \(T\).

It follows in particular that if \(G\) is not 4-colorable and \(\delta(G)\le B\), then
\[
 p_G(2B)>0.                                                           \tag{3}
\]
For if \(T\) is the endpoint set of an optimal coloring, then \(|T|\le2B\). Were \(\delta(G[T])=0\), the preceding four-color construction would apply. Hence \(0<\delta(G[T])\le p_G(2B)\).

## 2. A bounded witness for defect in bounded-diameter graphs

We need a uniform fact: if all connected components of a finite graph have bounded diameter and its defect exceeds \(t\), this excess is already visible on a bounded number of vertices. We give the full argument because its uniformity is important later.

Fix integers \(D,t\). Suppose every two vertices in the same component of \(H\) can be joined by a walk of length at most \(D\), and \(t<\delta(H)\).

For each component choose a root, and for every vertex \(v\) choose a root-to-\(v\) walk \(P_v\) of length at most \(D\). Let \(F\) be any set of at most \(t\) edges. Regard an edge in \(F\) as prescribing “equal endpoint bits” and an edge outside \(F\) as prescribing “different endpoint bits.” Along a walk, xor these prescribed changes. This defines a trial bit \(c_0(v)\) from the parity along \(P_v\).

Because \(\delta(H)>t\), the error set of \(c_0\) is not contained in \(F\). Choose a monochromatic edge \(ab\) for \(c_0\) that is not in \(F\). Set
\[
 R=\{ab\}\cup E(P_a)\cup E(P_b).
\]
Then \(|R|\le 2D+1\). We claim that whenever a two-coloring \(c\) has every edge of \(F\) monochromatic, it has some monochromatic edge in \(R\setminus F\).

Suppose not. On each root path \(P_a,P_b\), an edge is then monochromatic under \(c\) exactly when it is in \(F\): membership in \(F\) implies monochromaticity by assumption, while any monochromatic edge in \(R\) was assumed to belong to \(F\). Thus parity telescoping along the paths gives
\[
 c(\operatorname{root}(a))\oplus c(a)=c_0(a),\qquad
 c(\operatorname{root}(b))\oplus c(b)=c_0(b).
\]
Since \(a,b\) are adjacent, they have the same root. Since \(ab\) was monochromatic under \(c_0\), the displayed identities force \(c(a)=c(b)\). Thus \(ab\) itself is a monochromatic edge in \(R\setminus F\), a contradiction. This proves the claim.

We now use a finite branching argument. Its abstract form is this. Let \(\mathcal E\) be a family of finite subsets of some set. Assume that for every \(F\) with \(|F|\le t\), there is a set \(R_F\) of at most \(k\) elements such that every \(E\in\mathcal E\) containing \(F\) also contains an element of \(R_F\setminus F\). Then there is one finite set \(X\), of size bounded only in terms of \(k,t\), such that
\[
 |E\cap X|>t\quad\text{for every }E\in\mathcal E.                   \tag{4}
\]

Here is a direct construction. Starting from a partial set \(F\), branch over all possible new elements in \(R_F\setminus F\), insert the selected element, and continue until \(t+1\) selected elements have been forced. The depth is at most \(t+1\), and each node has at most \(k\) children, so the union of all elements appearing in this finite tree has a bound depending only on \(k,t\). More explicitly, one may define
\[
 b(k,t,0)=t+k,
 \qquad b(k,t,r+1)=t+k+k\,b(k,t,r).
\]
An induction on the remaining depth shows that a tree beginning with \(|F|+r=t\) can be supported on at most \(b(k,t,r)\) elements and forces more than \(t\) of those elements into every member of \(\mathcal E\) extending \(F\). Taking \(F=\varnothing,r=t\) gives (4).

Apply this with \(k=2D+1\) and with \(\mathcal E\) the error sets of all two-colorings of \(H\). The parity argument supplies the required \(R_F\). We obtain an edge set \(X\), with
\[
 |X|\le b(2D+1,t,t),

a such that every coloring has more than \(t\) errors among the edges of \(X\). Let \(U\) be the set of endpoints of edges in \(X\). Then
\[
 |U|\le W(D,t):=2b(2D+1,t,t),                                       \tag{5}
\]
and every two-coloring of \(H[U]\) has more than \(t\) monochromatic edges. Therefore
\[
 t<\delta(H[U]).                                                     \tag{6}
\]
This is the required bounded witness theorem.

## 3. Finite-source neighborhoods and height bands

Let \(G\) be finite, let \(S\subseteq V(G)\), and let \(R\ge0\). Define
\[
 N_R(S)=\{v:\text{some }s\in S\text{ has a walk to }v
                    \text{ of length at most }R\}.
\]
Define the truncated height
\[
 r(v)=\min\{q:v\in N_q(S)\},

a
\]
when such a \(q\le R\) exists, and put \(r(v)=R+1\) otherwise. Thus vertices in components disjoint from \(S\), as well as vertices farther than \(R\), receive the sentinel height \(R+1\). We have
\[
 r(v)=0\iff v\in S,
 \qquad |r(x)-r(y)|\le1\quad\text{whenever }xy\in E(G).             \tag{7}
\]
The latter follows by appending the edge \(xy\) to a shortest source walk, with the sentinel case immediate.

The components of \(G[N_R(S)]\) have a diameter bound depending on \(|S|\) and \(R\), but not on \(|V(G)|\):
\[
 D_S=|S|(2R+1).                                                       \tag{8}
\]
To prove this, every vertex of \(N_R(S)\) has a source walk of length at most \(R\), entirely inside the neighborhood. Build a contact graph on the roots \(S\), joining two distinct roots when they are connected in \(G[N_R(S)]\) by a walk of length at most \(2R+1\). A walk in a component of \(G[N_R(S)]\), together with source paths at its successive vertices, shows that the source roots associated with its endpoints lie in one component of this contact graph. A simple path in the contact graph has at most \(|S|-1\) edges. Expand each contact edge to a walk of length at most \(2R+1\), and append the two endpoint source paths. The resulting length is at most
\[
 R+(|S|-1)(2R+1)+R\le |S|(2R+1).
\]
Vertices outside the neighborhood are isolated in the restricted graph and cause no problem.

We also need a clean-band observation. If \(T\) has at most \(2B\) vertices, then among the \(2B+1\) disjoint four-layer bands
\[
 [N+1+4j,N+1+4j+4),\qquad 0\le j\le2B,
\]
one contains no height of a vertex in \(T\). Hence there exists \(a\) such that
\[
 N<a,
 \qquad a+3\le N+4(2B+1),                                           \tag{9}
\]
and
\[
 v\in T\implies r(v)<a\ \text{or}\ a+4\le r(v).                    \tag{10}
\]
This is just the pigeonhole principle: distinct bands are disjoint, so if all were occupied they would require at least \(2B+1\) marked vertices.

## 4. The two-vertex cap

We now describe the central replacement construction.

Let \(r:V(G)\to\mathbb N\) satisfy the edge-Lipschitz condition (7), fix a level \(a\), and fix a bit assignment \(\beta:V(G)\to\{0,1\}\). Form a graph
\[
 C=\operatorname{Cap}(G,r,a,\beta)

a
\]
on the vertex set \(V(G)\sqcup\{z_0,z_1\}\) as follows.

* Between old vertices \(x,y\), retain the edge \(xy\) exactly when
  \(r(x),r(y)<a\).
* Join an old vertex \(x\), with \(r(x)<a\), to \(z_i\) if there is an edge
  \(xy\in E(G)\) with \(r(y)=a\) and \(\beta(y)=i\).
* Join \(z_0\) to \(z_1\).
* Old vertices of height at least \(a\) have no edges in \(C\).

Assign bit \(\beta(x)\) to an old vertex and bit \(i\) to \(z_i\).

### 4.1 Exact cap defect

Suppose \(S\) is the height-zero source set, \(a\le R\), and \(\beta\) is an optimal coloring of \(G[N_R(S)]\) such that all its errors lie in \(G[S]\). Then
\[
 \delta(C)=\delta(G[S]).                                             \tag{11}
\]

For the upper bound, inspect the distinguished bit assignment just described. An edge between old vertices can be monochromatic only if the corresponding edge of \(G[N_R(S)]\) is a \(\beta\)-error, hence both endpoints lie in \(S\). A cap edge \(xz_i\), represented by an edge \(xy\) with \(r(x)<a,r(y)=a,\beta(y)=i\), cannot be monochromatic: otherwise \(\beta(x)=\beta(y)\), making \(xy\) an error in the neighborhood, so \(y\in S\); but then \(r(y)=0\), contrary to \(r(y)=a>0\). Finally, \(z_0z_1\) is not monochromatic. Thus all cap errors come from errors in \(G[S]\), proving \(\delta(C)\le\delta(G[S])\).

For the reverse inequality, the old vertices of \(S\), all of height zero, induce a copy of \(G[S]\) in \(C\). Defect cannot decrease when passing to a graph containing an injective copy, so \(\delta(G[S])\le\delta(C)\). This proves (11).

### 4.2 Small profile coordinates do not increase

Under the same concentration hypothesis, for every \(n<a\),
\[
 p_C(n)\le p_G(n).                                                   \tag{12}
\]

Fix a set \(U\subseteq V(C)\) with \(|U|\le n<a\), and let \(S_U\) be the old vertices of \(U\). Choose an optimal two-coloring \(c\) of \(G[S_U]\). We construct a coloring \(d\) of \(C[U]\).

Call a component of \(C[U]\) cap-reaching if it contains \(z_0\) or \(z_1\). On every cap-reaching component, use the distinguished cap bits \(\beta,i\). On every other component, use \(c\) on old vertices; a cap vertex cannot occur there by definition.

No cap-reaching component contains a source vertex. Indeed, define a potential on \(C\) by
\[
 \rho(x)=\min(r(x),a)\quad(x\text{ old}),\qquad \rho(z_i)=a.
\]
The cap definition and the Lipschitz property of \(r\) imply that \(\rho\) changes by at most one along an edge. If a source vertex, of potential zero, were connected within \(C[U]\) to a cap vertex, take a simple path. It would have length at least \(a\), whereas a simple path inside a set of fewer than \(a\) vertices has length less than \(a\), a contradiction.

Now inspect a monochromatic edge under \(d\). Its endpoints lie in the same component. In a non-cap-reaching component, both are old and its error is exactly an error of \(c\) in \(G[S_U]\). In a cap-reaching component, the distinguished cap assignment is used. Every error of that assignment maps to an error in \(G[S]\), as in the proof of (11), and hence would involve a source vertex. But no source lies in a cap-reaching component. Thus there are no errors there. Consequently
\[
 \delta(C[U])\le |\operatorname{Err}_{G[S_U]}(c)|
 =\delta(G[S_U])\le p_G(n).
\]
Taking the maximum over \(U\) proves (12).

### 4.3 Extending four-colorings through a clean band

We need one further property: under suitable hypotheses, every 4-coloring of \(C\) extends to a 4-coloring of \(G\).

Besides \(\beta\), let \(\sigma\) be another two-coloring of \(G\), and let \(T\) contain both endpoints of every \(\sigma\)-monochromatic edge. Assume the four-layer band is clean in the sense of (10), and put
\[
 O=\{x\in T:a+4\le r(x)\}.
\]
Assume \(G[O]\) is bipartite. Also assume that \(\beta\) is proper on edges whose two endpoints both have height \(a\). Then every 4-coloring of the cap extends to \(G\).

Let \(c\) be a proper 4-coloring of \(C\). The two cap vertices are adjacent, so their colors define an injective two-color palette
\[
 A(i)=c(z_i),\qquad i=0,1.
\]
The other two of the four colors form an injective palette \(B(0),B(1)\), disjoint from \(A\). Let \(\tau\) be a proper bipartition of \(G[O]\). Define a coloring \(d\) of \(G\) by
\[
 d(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 c(x),&r(x)<a,\\
 A(\beta(x)),&r(x)=a,\\
 A(\tau(x)),&r(x)>a\text{ and }x\in O,\\
 B(\sigma(x)),&r(x)>a\text{ and }x\notin O.
 \end{cases}                                                        \tag{13}
\]
We verify all cases for an edge \(xy\), orienting it so that \(r(x)\le r(y)\). By Lipschitzness, \(r(y)\le r(x)+1\).

* If \(r(x)<a\) and \(r(y)<a\), the edge is present between the corresponding old vertices of \(C\), so \(c(x)\ne c(y)\).
* If \(r(x)<a\le r(y)\), Lipschitzness forces \(r(y)=a\). The cap contains the edge from \(x\) to \(z_{\beta(y)}\), so again (13) gives different colors.
* If both heights equal \(a\), the assumed propriety of \(\beta\) at layer \(a\), together with injectivity of \(A\), separates them.
* If \(r(x)=a<r(y)\), then \(y\notin O\), because membership in \(O\) requires \(r(y)\ge a+4\). Thus \(x\) uses palette \(A\) and \(y\) palette \(B\), which are disjoint.
* Suppose both heights exceed \(a\). If both vertices are in \(O\), propriety of \(\tau\) separates their \(A\)-colors. If exactly one is in \(O\), the palettes \(A,B\) separate them. Finally, suppose neither lies in \(O\). If their \(B\)-colors were equal, injectivity of \(B\) would give \(\sigma(x)=\sigma(y)\), so both endpoints would lie in \(T\). Cleanliness says that each vertex of \(T\) is either below \(a\) or at height at least \(a+4\). Since \(r(x)>a\), this forces \(x\in O\), contrary to the case assumption.

Thus (13) is proper.

It remains to explain why \(\beta\) is proper at layer \(a\) in our application. If an edge \(xy\) at that layer had \(\beta(x)=\beta(y)\), the concentration of all \(\beta\)-errors in \(S\) would force \(x,y\in S\), hence height zero, contradicting \(a>0\).

Combining (11), (12), and this extension gives the cap lemma: if \(N<a\), then the cap has exact defect \(\delta(G[S])\), satisfies
\[
 p_C(n)\le p_G(n)\quad(n\le N),                                     \tag{14}
\]
and 4-colorability of \(C\) implies 4-colorability of \(G\).

## 5. A uniform plateau replacement

We now show that a sufficiently long plateau in \(p_G\) permits a cap replacement with a pointwise smaller profile.

For integers \(B,N\), define
\[
 R(B,N)=N+4(2B+1),
\]
\[
 D(B,N)=N(2R(B,N)+1),
\]
and
\[
 M(B,N)=\max\left\{N+2B,\ \max_{0\le t\le B}W(D(B,N),t)\right\},    \tag{15}
\]
where \(W\) is the bounded-witness function from (5). Plainly \(M(B,N)\ge N\).

Let \(G\) be finite, assume
\[
 \delta(G)\le B,
 \qquad p_G(N)=p_G(M(B,N)).                                          \tag{16}
\]
Choose \(S\) with \(|S|\le N\) and
\[
 \delta(G[S])=p_G(N).                                                \tag{17}
\]
We first prove that the whole radius-\(R(B,N)\) neighborhood of \(S\) is saturated:
\[
 \delta(G[N_R(S)])=p_G(N),
 \qquad R=R(B,N).                                                     \tag{18}
\]
The inequality “\(\ge\)” follows from \(S\subseteq N_R(S)\). If the left side were strictly greater than \(t=p_G(N)\), then every component of this neighborhood graph has diameter at most
\[
 |S|(2R+1)\le D(B,N).
\]
The bounded witness theorem would provide a vertex set \(U\) with
\[
 |U|\le W(D(B,N),t)\le M(B,N)

a
\]
and \(t<\delta(G[U])\). Here \(t=p_G(N)\le\delta(G)\le B\), so the relevant witness bound occurs in (15). But then
\[
 \delta(G[U])\le p_G(M(B,N))=p_G(N)=t,
\]
a contradiction. This proves (18).

Choose an optimal two-coloring \(\beta\) of \(G[N_R(S)]\). Equations (17) and (18), together with property 4 from Section 1, show that every \(\beta\)-monochromatic edge in the neighborhood has both endpoints in \(S\).

Next choose an optimal two-coloring \(\sigma\) of all of \(G\), and let \(T\) be the endpoints of its errors. By (2),
\[
 |T|\le2\delta(G)\le2B.
\]
Use the clean-band pigeonhole argument to choose \(a\) with
\[
 N<a,
 \qquad a+3\le R,

a
\]
and no vertex of \(T\) at any height \(a,a+1,a+2,a+3\). Set
\[
 T_{\rm out}=\{x\in T:a+4\le r(x)\}.
\]
The sets \(S\) and \(T_{\rm out}\) are disjoint, since vertices of \(S\) have height zero, and
\[
 |S\cup T_{\rm out}|\le N+2B\le M(B,N).
\]
By superadditivity (1), profile domination, (17), and the plateau equality,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 p_G(N)+\delta(G[T_{\rm out}])
 &=\delta(G[S])+\delta(G[T_{\rm out}])\\
 &\le\delta(G[S\cup T_{\rm out}])\\
 &\le p_G(M(B,N))=p_G(N).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
 \delta(G[T_{\rm out}])=0.                                         \tag{19}
\]

All hypotheses of the cap construction now hold. It produces a finite graph \(C\), on the old vertex set plus two cap vertices, such that
\[
 \delta(C)=p_G(N),                                                    \tag{20}
\]
\[
 C\text{ 4-colorable}\implies G\text{ 4-colorable},                 \tag{21}
\]
and, for \(n\le N\), \(p_C(n)\le p_G(n)\).

For every \(n\), moreover,
\[
 p_C(n)\le\delta(C)=p_G(N).                                         \tag{22}
\]
If \(n>N\), monotonicity gives \(p_G(N)\le p_G(n)\), so (22) also implies \(p_C(n)\le p_G(n)\). Combining this with the small-coordinate estimate yields the uniform plateau replacement conclusion
\[
 p_C(n)\le \min\{p_G(n),p_G(N)\}\quad\text{for every }n.            \tag{23}
\]
In particular, if \(G\) is not 4-colorable, then by (21) neither is \(C\).

## 6. An abstract avoiding staircase

Let \(\mathcal P\) be the family of profiles \(p_G\) of all finite graphs \(G\) that are not 4-colorable. Every \(p\in\mathcal P\) is nondecreasing and bounded: if \(p=p_G\), then
\[
 p(n)\le\delta(G)

a
\]
for every \(n\).

The preceding work gives two uniform properties.

* Positive detection: if \(p=p_G\in\mathcal P\) and \(p(n)\le B\) for all \(n\), then \(\delta(G)=p(|V(G)|)\le B\), and by (3),
\[
 p(2B)>0.                                                            \tag{24}
\]
Thus take \(d(B)=2B\).

* Plateau capping: if \(p\in\mathcal P\), \(p\le B\),
\[
 p(N)=p(M(B,N))>0,

a
\]
then the replacement graph above is still not 4-colorable and its profile \(q\in\mathcal P\) satisfies
\[
 q(n)\le\min\{p(n),p(N)\}\quad\text{for all }n.                    \tag{25}
\]

We now construct one nondecreasing divergent function that dominates no profile in \(\mathcal P\).

For fixed \(B\) and starting point \(s\), define samples
\[
 a_0=s,
 \qquad a_{i+1}=M(B,a_i).
\]
Because \(M(B,N)\ge N\), these indices are nondecreasing.

Define thresholds recursively by
\[
 L_0=0,

a
\]
and, for \(j\ge0\), put \(B=j+1\), start the \(B\)-sample sequence at
\[
 s=\max\{L_j,d(B)\},

a
\]
and set
\[
 L_{j+1}=a_B+1.                                                      \tag{26}
\]
Then \(L_j<L_{j+1}\). Define the inverse staircase
\[
 f(n)=\min\{j:n<L_{j+1}\}.                                         \tag{27}
\]
It is nondecreasing. It also tends to infinity: for every \(j\), if \(n\ge L_j\), then \(f(n)\ge j\). Thus eventually \(f(n)\) exceeds every prescribed integer.

We prove by induction on \(j\) the stronger assertion
\[
 \text{no }p\in\mathcal P\text{ satisfies }
 p(n)\le\min\{f(n),j\}\text{ for every }n.                         \tag{28}
\]

For \(j=0\), such a profile would be identically zero, contradicting positive detection (24) with \(B=0\).

Assume (28) for \(j\), and suppose for contradiction that
\[
 p(n)\le\min\{f(n),j+1\}\quad\text{for every }n                    \tag{29}
\]
for some \(p\in\mathcal P\). In particular \(p\le j+1\). Use the \(B=j+1\) sample sequence \(a_0,\ldots,a_B\) occurring in the construction of \(L_{j+1}\). All these indices satisfy
\[
 a_i<L_{j+1}.

a
\]
By the definition of the inverse staircase, \(f(a_i)\le j\). Hence (29) gives
\[
 p(a_i)\le j\qquad(0\le i\le B).                                  \tag{30}
\]
On the other hand, \(a_0\ge d(B)\), so monotonicity and (24) imply
\[
 p(a_0)>0.                                                          \tag{31}
\]
The nondecreasing integer sequence
\[
 p(a_0),p(a_1),\ldots,p(a_B)

a
\]
has \(B+1\) terms, begins positively, and ends at most \(j=B-1\) by (30). It therefore cannot strictly increase at every one of its \(B\) steps: strict increase at every step would make the final value at least \(1+B>B-1\). Thus for some \(i<B\),
\[
 p(a_i)=p(a_{i+1})=p(M(B,a_i))>0.                                   \tag{32}
\]
Apply plateau capping to obtain \(q\in\mathcal P\) with
\[
 q(n)\le\min\{p(n),p(a_i)\}.

a
\]
By (29), \(q(n)\le f(n)\), while (30) gives \(p(a_i)\le j\), so \(q(n)\le j\). Therefore
\[
 q(n)\le\min\{f(n),j\}

a
\]
for every \(n\), contradicting the induction hypothesis. This proves (28).

Finally, no \(p\in\mathcal P\) can satisfy \(p(n)\le f(n)\) for every \(n\). Indeed, each \(p\) is bounded by some \(B\); then it would satisfy
\[
 p(n)\le\min\{f(n),B\},

a
\]
contradicting (28) at \(j=B\).

We have therefore constructed a nondecreasing divergent \(f\) such that
\[
 \bigl(\forall n,\ p_G(n)\le f(n)\bigr)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad G\text{ is 4-colorable}                 \tag{33}
\]
for every finite graph \(G\).

## 7. Relating defect to the edge-deletion formulation

We now connect (33) to the quantities in the conjecture.

Let \(A\) be a finite subgraph. Its minimum number of edge deletions needed to become bipartite is exactly \(\delta(A)\).

For one inequality, choose any two-coloring \(c\) and delete precisely its monochromatic edges. Every remaining edge has differently colored endpoints, so the resulting graph is bipartite. Minimizing gives
\[
 \text{deletion distance}(A)\le\delta(A).

a
\]
Conversely, suppose deleting an edge set \(E\) makes \(A\) bipartite. Take a proper two-coloring of \(A-E\). Every edge of \(A\) monochromatic under this coloring must belong to \(E\). Hence
\[
 \delta(A)\le |E|.

a
\]
Minimizing over successful \(E\) proves equality.

The set of deletion distances of all finite \(n\)-vertex subgraphs of any graph is bounded by \(\binom n2\), so its supremum is well-defined as a natural number, even if there are no such subgraphs. Every actual finite \(n\)-vertex subgraph has deletion distance at most this supremum.

Now let \(G\), possibly infinite, satisfy the conjecture’s envelope for our constructed \(f\):
\[
 \operatorname{MaxDist}_G(n)\le f(n)\quad\text{for every }n,         \tag{34}
\]
where \(\operatorname{MaxDist}_G(n)\) denotes the supremum of the bipartite edge-deletion distances over finite \(n\)-vertex subgraphs.

Take any finite subgraph \(A\) of \(G\). For a set \(S\subseteq V(A)\) with \(|S|\le n\), regard the induced restriction \(A[S]\) as a subgraph of \(G\) whose vertex set is exactly \(S\), omitting the other isolated vertices. By the equality between defect and deletion distance and by (34),
\[
 \delta(A[S])
 \le \operatorname{MaxDist}_G(|S|)
 \le f(|S|)
 \le f(n),

a
\]
where the last inequality uses monotonicity of \(f\). Maximizing over all \(|S|\le n\) gives
\[
 p_A(n)\le f(n)\quad\text{for every }n.                             \tag{35}
\]
By (33), every finite subgraph \(A\) of \(G\) is 4-colorable.

A standard finite compactness argument now shows that \(G\) itself is 4-colorable. For completeness, consider the product space \(\{1,2,3,4\}^{V(G)}\). For each edge \(xy\), impose the closed condition that the two coordinates differ. Any finite collection of these conditions involves a finite subgraph, which has a proper 4-coloring, so the finite collection is satisfiable. Compactness of the product of finite discrete spaces gives a point satisfying all edge conditions simultaneously. Equivalently, one may apply the finite intersection principle to the sets of partial proper colorings. Thus \(G\) has a proper 4-coloring.

Consequently its chromatic number is at most 4 and in particular is not infinite.

## 8. Final contradiction

The function \(f\) constructed in Section 6 is nondecreasing and satisfies \(f(n)\to\infty\). Sections 7 and 6 show that every graph satisfying
\[
 \operatorname{MaxDist}_G(n)\le f(n)\quad\text{for all }n

a
\]
is 4-colorable. Therefore there is no graph of infinite chromatic number satisfying these bounds for this \(f\).

The conjectured statement asserts the existence of such an infinite-chromatic graph for every divergent \(f\). Applying it to the divergent function just constructed yields a contradiction. Hence the formalized assertion is false.
